newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan c.bank says won't cut reserve requirements.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan c.bank says won't cut reserve requirements.

text.p: Taiwan's central bank said on Tuesday it had no immediate plans to ease banks' reserve requirements despite tight liquidity in the banking system.

"At present, we do not have any plans to cut banks' reserve requirements because the current tight liquidity will not last long," Lee Sheng-yen, business director of the central bank, told reporters after the close of trading.

Lee made the comment when asked about a newspaper report saying the central bank was considering lowering reserve requirements to relieve an intense liquidity squeeze that has pushed short-term money rates to unusually high levels.

Lee also reiterated that the central bank had not considered injecting funds through open-market operations, though it would continue to tinker with liquidity through issues of negotiable certificates of deposit.
"The central bank will continue its routine action to have minor adjustment in the money market, but until now we still are not considering open-market operations," he said.
Taiwan's money rates continued high and volatile on Tuesday on tight liquidity after the central bank said late on Monday that it would not inject funds to ease the situation.

Despite its pledge not to inject funds through open market operations, dealers said the central bank did inject T$20 billion into the banking system on Tuesday through a novel closed approach, allowing a state bank to withdraw money it had redeposited in the central bank.
A central bank official said the central bank agreed to let the state-run Taiwan Cooperative Bank make the withdrawal to increase money market liquidity as short-term rates soared.
Dealers said the method had not been seen in Taiwan before, calling it a "closed market operation".
Such withdrawals require special central bank approval, dealers said.

Dealers said the move succeeded in bringing down the overnight interbank rate, which had rocketed to 9.103 percent against Monday's 8.323 close, in the mid-day session, but had retreated to 8.395 percent at the close.
Dealers said the main factor pushing rates higher was the red hot stock market, which continued to suck funds out of the banking system.
The rates would rise further if the stock market rally continued, especially at high turnover levels, they said.
The stock market has gained more than 700 points or almost nine percent in June despite easing slightly on Tuesday.
Tightening liquidity also helped push the recently depreciating Taiwan dollar to a firmer close on Tuesday.
The local unit closed at T$27.885 high against Monday's T$27.892 finish.
